clinicalPearls: The second most common subtype of renal cell carcinoma after clear cell disease
Often appears as a hypovascular renal mass, enhancing less avidly than clear cell tumours on contrast imaging
Frequently multifocal and bilateral, more so than other subtypes
Traditionally divided into type 1 and type 2, with type 2 generally behaving more aggressively
Hereditary forms include hereditary papillary renal carcinoma (MET) and hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer (fumarate hydratase)
A fumarate hydratase-deficient tumour should prompt genetic assessment because of its aggressive nature
Localised low-grade disease generally carries a good prognosis after surgery
reference.pathophysiology: Papillary renal cell carcinoma arises from the epithelium of the proximal or distal tubule and is characterised by papillary or tubulopapillary growth, often with foamy macrophages and haemosiderin. Type 1 tumours are frequently associated with gains of chromosomes 7 and 17 and, in hereditary cases, activating MET mutations. Type 2 tumours are more heterogeneous and include fumarate hydratase-deficient cancers linked to hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell cancer, which pursue an aggressive course. The relatively poor vascularity explains the characteristically modest enhancement on imaging.
additionalDifferentials: MiT family translocation renal cell carcinoma
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI to characterise and stage the mass
Renal mass biopsy where it will guide management
Immunohistochemistry and, where indicated, fumarate hydratase staining
Genetic assessment when hereditary features or syndromic signs are present
Chest imaging and baseline bloods for staging of larger tumours
redFlags: High-grade or type 2 histology, especially fumarate hydratase-deficient tumours
Locally advanced or metastatic disease at presentation
Cutaneous or uterine leiomyomas suggesting a hereditary syndrome
Rapid growth of a previously indolent lesion
reference.prognosis: Localised, low-grade type 1 tumours generally have a favourable prognosis after surgery; higher-grade type 2 and fumarate hydratase-deficient tumours carry a worse outlook with a greater risk of metastasis.
pitfalls: Assuming a hypovascular mass is benign because it enhances poorly
Missing a hereditary syndrome in a young patient with an aggressive type 2 tumour
Applying clear cell prognostic assumptions to papillary disease
references: WHO Classification of Urinary and Male Genital Tumours
management: Recognize type 1 (MET pathway driven, indolent) versus type 2 (CDKN2A/SETD2/TFE3-TFEB, more aggressive, worst with FH mutation/HLRCC) to guide treatment intensity and follow up

For small localised masses, choose between radical nephrectomy, partial nephron sparing nephrectomy, thermal ablation, or active surveillance based on size, location, comorbidity and renal function, led by a urologist experienced in kidney cancer
Favor partial nephrectomy for small renal masses when feasible to preserve renal parenchyma
Offer active surveillance with serial imaging every three to six months for selected patients, particularly small or complex cystic lesions or significant competing comorbidity
For locally advanced disease with venous or caval extension, proceed to surgery (radical nephrectomy with thrombectomy, escalating to vascular reconstruction as needed) regardless of histology
Reserve regional lymphadenectomy mainly as a staging tool in node negative disease, used selectively, but perform it as standard when nodes are radiographically involved

Treat adjuvant systemic therapy after resection as not clearly established for papillary histology outside a clinical trial, and individualise through a genitourinary oncology multidisciplinary team, favoring trial enrollment when available

In MET-driven papillary disease, consider MET pathway inhibition (such as foretinib) as a biologically rational but only modestly effective option, and test for MET mutation to help select likely responders

For metastatic disease without papillary-specific data, apply general RCC systemic therapy classes (VEGF pathway tyrosine kinase inhibitors, mTOR inhibitors, immune checkpoint inhibitor combinations) sequenced by risk group and prior therapy, discussed with a genitourinary oncology multidisciplinary team
Prefer clinical trial enrollment for metastatic papillary RCC given the limited histology-specific evidence base
Suspect a germline MET mutation and refer for genetic assessment when multifocal, bilateral type 1 tumours are seen, and offer relatives cascade testing and renal imaging surveillance

Suspect HLRCC in aggressive, typically solitary type 2 tumours with FH mutation, especially with personal or family history of cutaneous or uterine leiomyomas, and pursue prompt genetic referral with closer surveillance
Monitor postoperatively with cross-sectional chest and abdominal imaging timed and intensified by stage, grade and histologic risk, with higher intensity for type 2 or FH-deficient tumours

Refer to urology for any renal mass needing biopsy, surgical planning or ablation candidacy, and to a genitourinary oncology multidisciplinary team for locally advanced, adjuvant, or any metastatic disease decision
